claims.text: Under sustained loading, the multilayers progressively shift from interface-controlled dislocation pile-up to an activated dislocation-transmission regime.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order mediate the proposed transition to dislocation transmission.
The transition between dislocation blocking and transmission governs the rate and character of plastic deformation.
The proposed starting material is a nanoscale multilayer containing FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy phases.
The proposed starting interfaces are well-defined and coherent, with minimal pre-existing residual stress.
The samples will be subjected to sustained mechanical loading in a creep experiment with controlled temperature and strain-rate conditions.
Constant-strain-rate testing from room to moderately elevated temperature is expected to preserve the nanoscale structure and interface integrity.
Local compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and short-range order at multilayer interfaces modulate dislocation activity.
Initial loading causes dislocations to pile up at coherent interfaces.
As loading persists, lattice distortions and chemical inhomogeneity promote partial dislocation transmission across interfaces.
Partial dislocation transmission progressively accommodates plastic deformation.
The transition to partial transmission will increase the steady-state creep rate relative to the starting baseline.
The predicted transition will be accompanied by evolving strain gradients and dislocation structures at interfaces.
The baseline response consists of an elastic-to-limited-plastic transition with interfacial dislocation accumulation but no significant transmission.
At very high temperatures or extremely high strain rates, thermally activated mechanisms may override the proposed interface-controlled progression.
Failure to observe any transition from pile-up to dislocation transmission under sustained loading would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify a constant imposed strain rate, while the prediction and measurements require detecting an increase in steady-state creep rate. An imposed constant strain rate cannot itself increase; a constant-stress or constant-load creep protocol, or a stress-relaxation outcome under constant strain rate, would be needed.
